Otolaryngology · published research

Vocal fold wound

One rabbit injury study reported tissue changes consistent with reduced scar formation, including increased hyaluronic acid and lower collagen and inflammation. It does not demonstrate wound-healing benefit in patients.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One rabbit injury study reported tissue changes consistent with reduced scar formation, including increased hyaluronic acid and lower collagen and inflammation. It does not demonstrate wound-healing benefit in patients.

Summary of the Evidence

Two titles appear in the exact Voice > Vocal fold mapping, with one additional related cell publication identified through mapping. Together, the three publications include one human randomized study of healthy voice under loading, one rabbit injury study with a cell arm, and one separate human vocal-fold epithelial-cell study. No patient trial directly treats a vocal-fold wound or scar.

Human and clinical evidence

Torres et al. studied PBM during vocal loading in healthy volunteers. The report found only subtle changes in a voice-quality measure and did not study wound healing (2025). It therefore cannot establish whether PBM prevents or treats vocal-fold scar after injury or surgery.

Animal evidence

Lou et al. used a rabbit vocal-fold injury model and reported increased hyaluronic acid with reduced collagen and inflammatory findings after PBM, supporting a possible scar-modulation mechanism (2019). These are tissue-level outcomes in an animal model, not proof of better voice or wound closure in people.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

A human vocal-fold epithelial-cell study reported increased cell migration and proliferation after PBM (Lou et al. 2019). The rabbit publication also included an in-vitro cell arm.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The records involve distinct settings: healthy human vocal loading, rabbit injury, and cultured human epithelial cells. Wavelengths, dosimetry, and tissue exposure cannot be assumed equivalent across these settings. Future clinical work needs prespecified wound and scar outcomes, voice measures, and laryngeal safety monitoring.

Interpretation

Preclinical tissue and cell findings justify further study, but direct clinical evidence for vocal-fold wound healing is absent. The healthy-volunteer voice study does not fill that gap.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for preventing or treating vocal-fold scar in people No direct clinical wound-healing evidence
Publications and records3 relevant publications: 2 exact-category titles and 1 mapped cell study.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The mapped evidence includes rabbit injury and cell studies suggesting effects on migration, hyaluronic acid, collagen, or inflammation, but no clinical trial in vocal-fold wounds. A human randomized study examined vocal loading in healthy participants rather than wound repair. Animal and laboratory findings require prospective clinical testing before scar prevention can be inferred.

Publication and study types

  • Human1 randomized healthy-volunteer vocal-loading study, not a wound trial.
  • Animal1 (rabbit) injury study.
  • In-vitro2 arms across 2 publications.
  • No clinical trial of vocal-fold wound healing.
